hpos.resolution: Resolved by observation in WCCS-002. DataSynchronizer::data_sync_is_enabled() is implemented as 'yes' === get_option( ORDERS_DATA_SYNC_ENABLED_OPTION ) and the option row is absent, so it evaluates to false. At runtime custom_orders_table_usage_is_enabled() returns true and the active order data store is OrdersTableDataStore. HPOS is therefore ON with synchronization OFF, which is exactly the state the WCCS-002 acceptance requires.
hpos.placeholder_note: Deleting/creating orders in this state still produces a wp_posts row of type 'shop_order_placehold' for compatibility, even though the value itself is stored only in wp_wc_orders_meta. Any code that lists posts must not treat that placeholder as an order.

architecture_decisions.acceptance_basis: ADR-0001 to ADR-0004 introduce no new direction; they record decisions already fixed by ROADMAP.md sections 13, 12, 2/5/9 and 1, using the evidence gathered in WCCS-001 to WCCS-004. ADR-0005 to ADR-0008 are different and say so: each records a decision taken while executing a task. ADR-0005 determined how the preview reproduces the section 17 breakpoints inside a frame narrower than the window; ADR-0006 determined where and how section 7's protection of structurally required fields is enforced; ADR-0007 sustained section 428 outside the inspector by making the published and the enforced vocabularies one class; ADR-0008 kept section 8's capability limits from becoming validation errors that block the merchant. None contradicts the planning. Because their origin differs, all four are candidates for explicit ratification by the product owner.
open_questions_carried_forward: ADR-0003 records that ROADMAP.md sections 5 and 9 disagree on whether the two CNPJ check digits may themselves be alphanumeric. To be resolved in WCCS-028 against the official source.

F01.quality_gates: composer check runs phpcs, phpstan and phpunit; all green. npm run build, lint:js and check-types are green. The gates were proven non-decorative by inserting a deliberate violation, which both PHPCS and PHPStan caught.
F01.ci_note: The GitHub Actions workflow is syntactically valid, every command it runs passed locally, and it is now versioned in the plugin's own repository. It still has not run: the repository has no remote and no runner has picked it up.
F01.detail: WCCS-006 delivered the first implementation: plugin header, identity constants, PSR-4 autoloader that does not require Composer, requirements guard that keeps activation safe without WooCommerce, i18n wiring with a generated POT catalog, and a working frontend build with dependency extraction. Proven by 33 assertions. WCCS-007 delivered the domain: the public FieldTypeInterface contract, three registries (types, presets, validators) with collision diagnostics, a schema validator that rejects undeclared settings, the canonical FieldDefinition, and the 21 v1 field types registered through the same public API an external plugin uses. Proven by 38 assertions. WCCS-008 delivered persistence: a compare-and-swap schema repository (draft, published, bounded revision history, restore-as-new-revision), schema versioning with a migration history, and the administrative REST endpoints that map the repository outcome to 200/401/409/422. Proven by 38 assertions.

F02.title: Design system e shell administrativo
F02.gate: Biblioteca visual aprovada em três larguras e com navegação por teclado.
F02.detail: WCCS-011 produced the design tokens the planning referenced but which never existed on disk: resources/design-tokens/tokens.json is now canonical, with matching CSS custom properties scoped to .wccs-admin and .wccs-checkout. 33 contrast pairs are measured by a unit test against WCAG 2.2 AA floors and none fails. WCCS-012 delivered the first real screen: a submenu under WooCommerce with the eight sections the planning fixes, assets gated to that screen alone, and a responsive shell whose breakpoints are checked against the tokens. WCCS-013 delivered the component library — Button, IconButton, Dialog, Tabs, Notice, Badge, StatusBadge, CompatibilityBadge, Field, the four controls, ErrorSummary and EmptyState — proven by a JavaScript suite that renders them in jsdom and operates them with real keyboard events. jsdom 26 does not implement the modal API of <dialog>, so focus containment is explicitly deferred to WCCS-063. The JSDoc-with-checkJs approach is a documented dead end for components that forward arbitrary native attributes; migrating the components to TypeScript is scheduled for F03, as section 18 of the planning intends. WCCS-014 delivered the REST client: error classification that keeps 403/409/422 distinct instead of flattening them into 'something failed', retries restricted to reads (a retried write would manufacture a conflict the user never caused), out-of-order response rejection, and an unsaved-work guard removed as soon as the work is saved. Proven by 18 JavaScript tests and 16 assertions. WCCS-015 delivered the visual preview, and its central problem was honesty rather than layout: narrowing a wrapper and calling it 'mobile' would have satisfied the acceptance while still rendering the desktop layout, because viewport media queries keep answering to the browser window. The frame therefore establishes a named inline-size query container and drives its width from design tokens per device class, so previewed content reflows with the frame; content that only has viewport rules does not reflow, and the frame says so through a mandatory capability surface rather than rendering a preview that looks complete. The preview introduced no REST route and reads nothing, proven by an assertion that the route set is unchanged and by a fetch spy that is never called. 20 new JavaScript tests, 24 assertions. See ADR-0005.
F02.why_gate_is_open: The gate has two halves and only one is satisfied. Keyboard navigation is proven: the JavaScript suite renders the shell and the component library in jsdom and operates them with real keyboard events, and the stylesheet declares a focus ring for every interactive element. The other half, 'aprovada em três larguras', has not been observed: no browser was opened in this phase, so no one has seen the layout at any of the three widths, let alone approved it. The preview now makes that reflow mechanically checkable — the container-query wiring is verified in the shipped bundle — but a verified mechanism is not a visual approval.
F02.way_forward: Two items close the gate and both belong to WCCS-063 (F10): a real-browser visual review at the desktop, tablet and mobile widths, and the accessibility audit, which is also where the deferred <dialog> focus containment lands. Phase F03 may proceed meanwhile because it depends on the component library's contracts, not on the visual sign-off.

defects_found_and_fixed: Field.js documented help, error and required as mandatory in JSDoc, so under strict checkJs the component was unusable by any consumer. Latent since WCCS-013 and only exposed when the preview became Field's first caller.

The preview stage centred a scroll container with justify-content: center, which clips the start edge and would have put the left of a 1280px preview permanently out of reach on a narrower admin screen.

The selector-scope parsers in the WCCS-012 and WCCS-013 harnesses used } as the only boundary, so the first selector inside every at-rule block escaped the check while the harness reported full coverage. Fixed in both by treating { as a boundary as well.

F03.title: Field Manager, seções e publicação
F03.gate: Lojista monta e publica um formulário completo, restaura revisão e não perde trabalho em conflito.
F03.why_gate_is_open: Every part of the gate is proven at the seam level: a merchant can assemble fields and sections, order them, configure each type, publish with a diff, validation and incompatibilities, restore a revision, and keep their work through a 409. But the gate describes an end-to-end action — 'Lojista monta e publica um formulário completo' — and no merchant has performed it, because no browser was opened in this phase. Proven at every joint and performed by someone are different claims, and the gate asks for the second.
F03.way_forward: Two things close it and both are already scheduled: the browser review in WCCS-063 (F10), which is also where the deferred <dialog> focus containment and the three-width visual approval of F02 land, and the end-to-end proof in F12. F04 may proceed meanwhile: it depends on the schema contracts, which are proven, not on visual approval.
F03.detail: WCCS-016 delivered the field picker and the CRUD over the draft, and three findings shaped it; all three are recorded in docs/validation/WCCS-016.md. (1) The first version read WooCommerce's checkout fields during plugins_loaded to build the validator. WooCommerce builds its countries object later, so that read was a fatal error which took down the front end, the admin and WP-CLI alike; function_exists('WC') is true long before WooCommerce exists, so it was the wrong readiness check. It was fixed by waiting for did_action('woocommerce_init'), by catching Throwable around the read, by refusing to cache an unavailable read (a memoised empty list would silently disable the origin rule) and by constructing the repository inside the rest_api_init callback. (2) The REST client never included the namespace: it asked /wp-json/schema/draft while the registered route is /wp-json/wc-checkoutsuite/v1/schema/draft. That was latent since WCCS-014 and hidden because the JavaScript test fixture baked the namespace into the root, which is not what the server sends. (3) The origin rule lived only in DefinitionValidator, which runs at publication, so a forged declaration could be parked in the draft; the rule was extracted so the repository applies it on every draft write as well. The picker is driven by the registry, so a third-party type appears with no change to the admin: 21 types in 7 categories, 12 presets, and the 20 real core fields of this store, read live through woocommerce_checkout_fields rather than from a hard-coded list. Core protection lives in CoreFieldGuard at the single persistence choke point and is proven through the real route: removal, archiving, retyping, relaxing a requirement and re-declaring the origin each return 422 with a stable code, while renaming, moving and resizing a core field is accepted — the limit of the rule is asserted, not only the rule. The TypeScript migration scheduled for F03 started where it pays (resources/admin/app/schema/types.ts and fieldOperations.ts) with no build configuration change, and the component library keeps its JSDoc migration for later. WCCS-017 delivered the inspector, whose requirement is one sentence about the whole system: show only the properties a field supports. An inspector that hides a control while the server accepts the value behind it satisfies the screenshot and not the requirement, so the work was split into three halves and all three are proven. The controls for a type are generated from the settingsSchema it declares, so a third-party type gets an editor with no change to the admin. Three real gaps were found: mask was stored and never read or validated (a schema could reference a mask that does not exist); storage and visibility were free maps, so 'redis' was a valid scope and 'twitter' a valid audience; and SchemaValidator did not know items, so the only requirement on an option was that the list had between 1 and 500 entries — the string 'banana' passed. minItems was declared on options since F01 and never read either. DefinitionVocabulary became the single source of every closed set, read by the validator and published to the client, with accepted values derived from the labelled lists rather than written twice; the integration proof compares the two arrays directly and asserts both directions, that every published value is accepted and every off-list value is refused. A mask reference is now {key, version} and the version must match the registered one, which is what makes the version Mask already carried mean something. description was added to the definition: ROADMAP.md section 7 requires descriptions and section 4 repeats them, but there was nowhere to keep one. The Conditions tab is absent on purpose: section 428 fixes six inspector groups and the sixth belongs to F06, so the tab appears only once there is an engine behind it rather than as a panel that opens onto nothing. See ADR-0007. WCCS-018 delivered sections and ordering, and closed two gaps that had been open since F01: sections were stored without ever being validated, and a field's section was never checked against anything, so a field could belong to a section that does not exist and be configured, saved and rendered nowhere. The valid targets are the declared sections plus the five domain locations of section 4, which are always valid because a WooCommerce field adopted from the inventory already carries one. Section locations are modelled as logical places rather than slots, which is what section 4 warns about, and the rules and insertion mapping it also lists were deliberately not modelled: the rules are the conditions engine (F06) and the mapping belongs to the adapter (F04), and a key nothing reads is a promise the code does not keep. Ordering is proven as a storage claim — send an order, read it back, send the reverse, read it back — because a pure function proved in isolation says nothing about whether the order survives. Positions are renumbered on every move rather than swapped, so no ties are left behind and the saved order is the order that was chosen. The reorderable list offers buttons, announces the new position in a live region, and restores focus to the same item after each move, falling back to the opposite control when the one that was used became disabled at the end of the list; 19 DOM specs use a harness that really reorders, because a spy would leave the order intact and a reorder that never happens cannot lose focus. IconButton gained ref forwarding, without which focus management is impossible for whoever uses it. A real bug was found by the integration proofs: validate_references read the raw section key while FieldDefinition::from_array defaults an omitted one to 'order', so the same document was valid to the model and invalid to the check — the same two-sources-for-one-fact class as ADR-0007. Fixed at the root, with two regression tests. Pointer drag-and-drop is deliberately not implemented, and the accessibility reasoning for the keyboard path is recorded in docs/validation/WCCS-018.md rather than in an ADR: it is a reversible interface convention, not an architectural constraint, and adding it to the ADR set would dilute it. WCCS-019 delivered the publication surface. "Saving a draft does not affect the store" is proven on the stored documents rather than on what the interface shows: a document is published, a different draft is saved on top of it, and the published document is read back and compared byte for byte. The report answers three separate questions, which section 428 asks for and which lead to opposite actions: what will change (SchemaDiff), whether the schema is valid (422 on publish), and whether a checkout will honour it as written (PublishIncompatibilities). They are returned under separate keys so the interface cannot merge them by accident. The second is what gives the third its value: a valid draft can have incompatibilities, and blocking publication for a platform limitation the Suite can still answer would turn every gap in the Block checkout into a wall for the merchant. See ADR-0008. The capability matrix of section 8 became executable data rather than prose, and the Block answer is not an opinion: WCCS-003 verified against the installed WooCommerce 11.1.0 that the additional-fields API registers exactly text, select and checkbox, and that date is not among them, so the reason shown in the interface is that verification. Today's list of Block incompatibilities is therefore the list of what F07 must deliver, unsoftened. A second family is reported too: a core override whose WooCommerce field has gone, which is the drift ADR-0001 chose to be able to detect, reported only when the inventory was actually read. One difference is reported once rather than once per field below it: moving the first of twenty fields renumbers nineteen positions and is still one decision. Publication remains a single POST with compare-and-swap and the report is a read, because a read route that published would be the easiest way to change a store by accident. Two of my own defects were found by the proof itself: count() over a variable that was already an integer killed the harness after section 7, so sections 8 and 9 never ran, the cleanup never happened and each run inherited the previous run's draft — which surfaced first as a failure in an earlier section for an unrelated reason; and the proof was sending only the field it cared about instead of the whole document, the way a client does, which correctly tripped core_field_removed. Both fixed, and the proof is now verified to be idempotent across consecutive runs. An assertion from F02-015 that pinned the schema route count at four was rewritten without weakening it: it now asserts that the controller publishes exactly the paths it declares as constants and that none renders the preview. WCCS-020 delivered the states, bulk actions and local undo, and closed the last of the four parts of the gate at the seam level. Before it, four of the five states named in the acceptance reached the screen as error.message — a string, which is the same shape for all of them. The classifier turns them into distinct results with distinct remedies, and every one of them keeps the work, which is the rule ROADMAP.md section 428 states as 'falha não descarta trabalho'. The server half of that rule is proven too: a refused write changes nothing at all. A real defect was found while writing the classifier and it was in the worst possible place: ApiError exposes its classification as getters, not methods, and the code from WCCS-016 called them as functions — so the branch that handled a failed save threw a TypeError of its own, exactly when a merchant most needs to know what happened. No test caught it because no test exercised a failing save in the screen; it surfaced because the client tests used property access and the screen used calls. Fixed in four places, and the classifier's fixtures now build ApiError through its real constructor, because a fixture that builds the object differently from production tests something else. A third honesty gap was closed: a document written by a newer build decoded as empty, indistinguishable from a fresh install, so the screen said 'no fields yet' while the fields existed invisibly. read_status() now distinguishes absent, readable, unsupported_version and corrupt, and the proof asserts the state and the empty read side by side. This is the third instance in this phase of the same principle — two different situations must not look identical — after ADR-0007 and ADR-0008; it was recorded in the validation document rather than as a fourth ADR, and it is now a checklist item for later phases: every new storage slot must be able to report its own state. Local undo is separate from the publication history in the type, not in a comment: saving resets it, because after a save the server is the authority and undoing into a state the server never had would be a lie. The proof failed first for the third round in a row on the same family of mistake — inherited state between sections — and was fixed by establishing the state explicitly; it is now verified idempotent across consecutive runs.

defects_found_and_fixed: Reading WooCommerce's checkout fields during plugins_loaded was a fatal error that took down the whole site, including WP-CLI. Found by running a command, not by review.

The REST client built /wp-json/schema/draft instead of /wp-json/wc-checkoutsuite/v1/schema/draft: the namespace was published into the page and never used. Latent since WCCS-014 and hidden by a test fixture that baked the namespace into the root.
core_field_origin_required was enforced only at publication, so a definition claiming a WooCommerce id as custom could be parked in the draft. Found by the WCCS-016 integration proof.
mask was stored on every definition and never read or validated, so a schema could reference a mask that does not exist. Found by reading the domain before writing the inspector.

SchemaValidator had no items support and never enforced minItems, so the only requirement on a choice field's options was that the list had 1 to 500 entries of any shape. Both are now declared and enforced.

storage and visibility were free maps: any string was a valid scope and any key a valid audience, so a client could write scope 'redis' or expose a value to a nonexistent audience and nothing complained.

SectionValidator::validate_references read the raw `section` key while FieldDefinition::from_array defaults an omitted one to 'order', so the same document was valid to the definition model and invalid to the reference check simultaneously. Found by two integration proofs failing at once (F01-008 returned 409 instead of 422, F03-017 rejected an ordinary field). Fixed by resolving the section through the definition model.
sections were stored without ever being validated since F01: no id rule, no title requirement, no duplicate detection, no location check.
IconButton could not forward a ref, which made focus management impossible for any component that needed to restore focus after a DOM rewrite.

The WCCS-019 proof called count() on a variable that was already an integer, which was a fatal TypeError. It killed the harness after section 7, so the cleanup in section 9 never ran and every subsequent run inherited the previous run's draft — surfacing first as a failure in an earlier, unrelated section. Fixed, and the proof is now verified idempotent.

The WCCS-019 proof saved only the field it was interested in rather than the whole document the way a client does, which removes every other field including core overrides; the guard refused correctly and the proof was reading state it had not written.

ApiError exposes isForbidden, isConflict, isValidationFailure and isTransient as getters, not methods. The code from WCCS-016 called them as functions, so the branch handling a failed save threw a TypeError of its own at exactly the moment a save fails. Found while writing the classifier; no test exercised a failing save in the screen.

The classifier's own test fixture built ApiError as new ApiError(status, body) instead of new ApiError({status, data}), so every error classified as generic. A fixture that builds the object differently from production tests something else.

A document written by a newer build decoded as empty, indistinguishable from a fresh install, so the screen would say 'no fields yet' while the fields existed invisibly. SchemaRepository::read_status() now reports absent, readable, unsupported_version and corrupt.
Bulk move-to-section interleaved the moved fields where they were instead of appending them the way moving a single field does. Fixed so both do the same thing.

The WCCS-020 proof assumed a draft existed in section 5 after section 3 had deleted it, so both the 'someone else saves first' step and the assertion that followed failed silently on inherited state. Third consecutive task with this family of mistake; the proof is now verified idempotent.

REGRESSION reported by the user after the task was reported complete: the Fields tab rendered nothing. useDocumentHistory returned a new object on every render, the screen's loading effect depended on that object, and the effect re-ran after each of its own updates until React aborted. The screen had no test at all, which is why it shipped; tests/js/screens/FieldsScreen.test.js now renders it and its first assertion is that it loads exactly once. Verified the guard works by reintroducing the bad dependency: five tests fail with it and all pass without.

sectionHref dropped the origin from the address it returned, because it was assembled from pathname, query and hash. Fixed to keep the origin: the function returns an address, and an address without one is only usable by a caller that already knows where it is.

gate_evidence.assemble: WCCS-016 to WCCS-018: field picker and CRUD, per-type inspector, sections and ordering, all proven through the real routes and the DOM
gate_evidence.publish: WCCS-019: the report answers what will change, whether the schema is valid and whether a checkout will honour it; publication is a single CAS write
gate_evidence.restore: WCCS-019: an earlier revision is published again as a new revision and the history grows instead of losing an entry
gate_evidence.keep_work_through_conflict: WCCS-020: a 409 names the winning revision, writes nothing at all, and the merchant can save again by acknowledging it
gate_evidence.not_observed: No browser was opened, so no one has assembled and published a form through the interface

F04.title: Classic Checkout e persistência canônica
F04.gate: Pedidos Classic válidos e inválidos testados em HPOS on/off, visitante/logado e carrinho físico/virtual.
F04.why_gate_is_open: All five tasks of the phase are complete and every part of the gate is proven at a seam. Orders are created and their typed values verified on both order backends; validation is proven through WooCommerce's own posted-data filter and its own error collection; the schema-to-form translation is proven against the field array WooCommerce really builds. What the gate asks for and none of this provides is a checkout: this store has no page carrying the [woocommerce_checkout] shortcode, so no order has been created by a checkout, and two of the gate's variables — guest versus logged-in, and a physical versus virtual cart — are properties of a checkout request that cannot be produced without one. That is the open decision CLASSIC-TEST-SURFACE.
F04.way_forward: One decision closes what can be closed: CLASSIC-TEST-SURFACE. Either a test page with the checkout shortcode is created, or a decision is recorded that the Classic surface is proven at the filter, validation, order-creation and client-lifecycle layers instead of through a rendered page. Creating or repointing a page is outside the plugin root and needs authorisation. F05 may proceed meanwhile, exactly as F04 did, because every seam it builds on is proven; but it is the last phase for which that is comfortable, since from F05 on each phase adds behaviour a customer sees on the checkout. The rendered-page and end-to-end portion belongs with WCCS-063 (F10) and F12, where a browser is opened. One recorded follow-up also remains: a read-only schema read builds a definition validator it never uses, which reads and memoises a half-filtered core field inventory from inside the checkout filter.
F04.detail: WCCS-021 delivered the Classic adapter: the translation from the published schema to the array WooCommerce builds the checkout from. It is a pure function over the schema — apply(fields, definitions, sections) returns the filtered array plus a report — and a thin registration half that hooks woocommerce_checkout_fields at priority 20 and reads the published document only. The design decision that gives the task its value is what it does with a type it cannot render. Four of the twenty-one registered types (file, heading, paragraph, html) and two others (multiselect, checkbox-group) have no classic counterpart; rendering them as text would produce a field that collects something the store does not save, so they are skipped and reported, and the report is fired on wccs_classic_adapter_report for the diagnostic surface to read. Five more (number, url, date, time, datetime) render as text and are reported as degraded rather than as honoured. The distinction is asserted in both directions: a type that cannot render is absent from the output, and the report says why. Sections map to their homonyms except contact, which maps to billing because the classic checkout has no contact step — section 4 warns that the five concepts are not identical slots in every checkout, and a declared section uses its location rather than its id. Widths are honest about the grid WooCommerce actually has: 12 becomes form-row-wide, 6 becomes form-row-first and form-row-last alternating within each section, and 3 and 4 become form-row-wide plus a wccs-col-<n> class, because section 8 places widths in scoped CSS instead of promising grid control; the stylesheet that interprets those classes belongs to WCCS-046 and the classes are emitted without it. The core-field claim is proven against the live array this store builds rather than against a fixture: label, priority, class, required and autocomplete are compared before and after, and the strongest form of the claim is that the adapter preserves a contract it never writes — it cannot break a key it does not assign, and the proof asserts that no contract key appeared from nowhere. The assertion that ties F03 to F04 is that a draft is invisible here: a draft that adds a field and renames a core field leaves the checkout byte for byte as it was, so the draft/published separation would not be decorative at the one place it matters. Two defects were mine: fourteen instances of '} );' where '}' belonged were a parse error, and the way I had been invoking PHPUnit — with error_reporting=0 and display_errors=0, flags I had adopted to silence WP-CLI's deprecations and then carried into every PHP command — made it exit 255 having printed zero bytes, so the gate failed with an invisible cause. The flags are now confined to WP-CLI; the quality tools run without them. A gate that fails silently is worse than no gate, because it looks like it is working. WCCS-022 delivered the other half of the transaction: normalization and final validation of what was submitted. Two hooks, both server-side, and the choice of each is part of the answer. woocommerce_checkout_posted_data runs inside get_posted_data(), before the session is updated and before anything is validated, and its return value is the array the whole checkout works from — so it is the only place where a normalized value becomes the value the store acts on. woocommerce_after_checkout_validation hands over the WP_Error that process_checkout() turns into customer-facing notices, and the id carried with each error becomes the data-id attribute that WooCommerce's own checkout script uses to link the message to the field and place it inline beside it. The acceptance's first half, that an adulterated POST fails without JavaScript, is proven twice: four values no browser would submit are refused by a harness running under WP-CLI with no browser anywhere, and the harness reads WordPress's own hook registry to assert that the storefront half of this plugin is exactly three hooks and nothing else, with no script of its own on the request. There is no client-side half whose absence could matter. Four decisions went against the obvious, and one of them was a real defect avoided rather than fixed. CheckboxFieldType normalizes an unchecked box to false, and carrying that false back into WooCommerce's posted data looks exactly like integrating normalization — but WooCommerce represents unchecked as the empty string and decides requiredness with '' === $data[$key], and '' === false is false, so an unchecked required consent box would have passed while the Suite's own requiredness check also saw false as present. Both layers would have let a forged request through, which is the exact attack the acceptance names. The fix is a rule: only a textual canonical value is carried back, because the Suite contributes textual normalization at this seam and the typed canonical form belongs to order persistence, where WCCS-023 proves zeros and false are preserved. Requiredness is computed and deliberately not reported: WooCommerce enforces it from the same field array the form was built from, and it alone knows which fieldsets this request skips — maybe_skip_fieldset() turns shipping off when the customer is not shipping elsewhere, so a second opinion here would reject a correct customer. The proof asserts both halves, calling WooCommerce's real protected validate_posted_data() through a subclass rather than reimplementing it: WooCommerce refuses the empty required field and names the same id, the Suite adds no second message, and exactly one message is produced for that field. Only the fields the form carried are examined, tested by membership of the posted data rather than by the definition list, so a forged key for a field the adapter could not render disappears with WooCommerce's own building of the array, and an unrenderable required field blocks nobody. And the pipeline runs once per submission rather than once per hook: a second run on the already-normalized value would judge a forged 3000-character value under the shortened length a mask produced and quietly lose the length error. Extracting PublishedDocument turned up one finding, recorded rather than fixed: SchemaRepository::read() never uses the validator the constructor demands, so every read builds one, and inside woocommerce_checkout_fields that reads and memoises a core field inventory taken before WooCommerce applies the filter — the assignment of $this->fields happens before apply_filters, which is what prevents the infinite recursion and also what makes the memo half-filtered. No incorrect behaviour today, since only validate_origin() reads that memo and only on a schema write; real cost, and a follow-up for the F04 gate. WCCS-023 delivered the storage authority of ADR-0001. OrderFieldsService is the single point that knows the shape of _wccs_fields — a JSON string carrying {format, values} — and everything goes through WC_Order, so the backend stays WooCommerce's decision and the same code is correct with HPOS on and off. The schema revision is stored beside the values rather than inside them, because it is meaningful on its own and is what WCCS-024 needs to read an old order after a field changed. The authority rule lives at the write chokepoint rather than at the caller: values are filtered through the published definitions, so a field WooCommerce owns or a Blocks additional field never reaches this storage even when a caller passes it. The proof exercises both, and also asserts that no meta is written in the WooCommerce namespace — the _wc_other/ duplication that section 25 calls a high risk and that acceptance criterion 10 of V1 is about. The legacy backend was exercised by overriding WooCommerce's own woocommerce_order_data_store filter above the controller that sets it, a plugin-local and reversible override removed in the same run; it selects the data path the HPOS-off configuration uses, and deliberately does not change the store's authority, which is a site setting outside the plugin root and a migration rather than a test. The proof found one real defect that review would not have: json_encode(0.0) produces 0, so a zero of type float was stored as an integer and read back as one — precisely the 'zeros preserved' the acceptance names, invisible to any assertEquals because 0 == 0.0. Fixed with JSON_PRESERVE_ZERO_FRACTION, pinned by an assertion on both backends and explained where the flag lives. Three other failures were the harness being wrong rather than the code: two meta-row counts that assumed the plugin's key was the only row on the order, now counted by key, and one assertion that WooCommerce's own billing field would be populated, when the harness fires only the creation action and setting the native field is WC_Checkout::create_order()'s job — the harness now sets it the way that method does, so the assertion proves what it was meant to: the Suite writes to the order without touching the field WooCommerce owns. The storage slot was built with the state report the WCCS-020 checklist requires — absent, readable, unsupported_format, corrupt — so a payload from a newer build is never shown as an empty order. The payload uses a format version for the same reason. One WCCS-022 assertion had to be updated: it pins the storefront half to an exact hook set, this task legitimately added a fourth, and the pinning is what made the growth deliberate rather than silent. WCCS-024 delivered the historical reading. An order now carries its own minimal record — label, type and the option labels — and that record answers when the schema has moved on, which is what keeps 'renaming or archiving a field does not make an old order unreadable' true. The proof places one order and moves the schema underneath it five times, reading again after each and never writing to the order: every label renamed, an option relabelled, a field retyped from text to number, a field archived and a field removed from the document entirely. After all of it the stored payload is byte for byte what it was, which is section 13's 'do not mass-modify historic orders just to change a label' asserted rather than promised. The reading distinguishes where the label came from (snapshot, schema, or nothing) from whether the schema still agrees, because a renamed field is snapshot-and-current and nothing is wrong, while a retyped field is snapshot-and-not-current and that is exactly what a reader must not paper over. A value nothing can name is returned with its identifier and an empty type rather than hidden, and the type is empty rather than guessed at text, because inventing a type formats a number as text and produces a reading nobody authorised. The task had to decide something the planning left open: sections 5 and 13 say a type change requires a migration rather than a panel edit, which can mean refusing the change or keeping history readable. It was decided the second way and recorded as ADR-0010, with the reasons — the snapshot makes the change safe, refusing would cost the merchant real work to avoid a problem that no longer exists, and nothing in the plugin rewrites an order. The format marker added in WCCS-023 paid for itself: the payload moved from format 1 to 2 and format 1 is still read, so a payload written before the snapshot reads as an order that remembers its values but not their names, and format 3 is still refused. A three-reader duplication was closed on the way: the value-to-label map of the options was built inside the adapter, interpreted again by the choice type and needed a third time by the snapshot, so it became FieldDefinition::options() and all three read the same one. WCCS-025 delivered the client half, which is the one part of this phase that is not PHP. The contract is one sentence: a component starts once per element, not once per refresh. Identity is per node, not per identifier or selector, which is what makes 'was this already started?' the same question as 'did this element survive the refresh?' — and that single question answers both halves of the acceptance, because an element the registry has never seen is by definition one that was just replaced, the only case where a value can have been lost. The value keeper captures on update_checkout and restores on updated_checkout, only ever into a replacement, and never overwrites a value the server rendered into the new node: that is not a loss, and writing over it would be the client inventing an answer. It deliberately dispatches no events, because WooCommerce recalculates on change and a restore that announced itself would ask for a refresh that replaces the element and restores again. The server marks its own fields with data-wccs-field so the client can tell them apart — the identifier a merchant chose is not a pattern anything could match on — and marks only custom fields, because WooCommerce repopulates its own from the session and marking one would put a key on a core field that the adapter's rule says it does not touch. The bundle is gated twice, on the screen and on whether the published schema has anything the classic checkout can render, and a third time on the artifact existing: enqueuing a URL that was never built puts a 404 in the checkout and changes nothing else, while what the bundle does is an improvement on a checkout that already works without it. The positive path is asserted by handing both gates in — the same affordance the administration assets take for the same reason, since a gate nobody can exercise is a gate nobody has checked — and the build's own manifest proves the import was externalised to the WordPress jQuery rather than bundled. Two defects were found. In the harness, the helper that checks a hook was registered looked only for instance methods, so it reported a static registration as missing while the hook was plainly there; it now accepts both callable shapes. In the product, the WCCS-021 assertions that pinned a custom field's custom_attributes to an exact array failed when the marker joined them, and were rewritten to assert by key with a named assertion for the marker. That is the third task running in which an assertion pinning an exact value caught a deliberate change and forced it to be acknowledged, after the hook set in WCCS-023 and the payload format in WCCS-024.

defects_found_and_fixed: Fourteen occurrences of '} );' instead of '}' in the WCCS-021 unit test file were a PHP parse error.

PHPUnit had been invoked with -d error_reporting=0 -d display_errors=0 since the WP-CLI deprecation work, which made it exit 255 while printing nothing at all. The cause of that failure was invisible until the suppression was removed. The flags are now used only for WP-CLI commands; phpunit, phpcs and phpstan run without them.

The WCCS-021 integration proof established its state explicitly instead of inheriting it, after the same family of mistake in three consecutive tasks (WCCS-018, WCCS-019, WCCS-020); it is verified idempotent across consecutive runs.

Carrying a normalized boolean back into WooCommerce's posted data would have disabled its required check for a checkbox: it compares '' === $data[$key] and false is not '', while the Suite's own is_absent(false) is false by design because false is a real stored value. A forged POST with a required consent box left unchecked would have been accepted by both layers. Avoided before shipping by the rule that only a textual canonical value is carried back; the unit test asserts both that the pipeline normalized it and that what travels back is still the empty string.

Reporting requiredness from the Suite would have duplicated WooCommerce's message for an ordinary required field and rejected a correct customer for a fieldset WooCommerce deliberately skips, which maybe_skip_fieldset() does for shipping when the customer is not shipping elsewhere. The pipeline still computes it; the layer declines to report it, and the proof asserts the two halves together — WooCommerce refuses and names the field, the Suite adds nothing, one message is produced.

Judging the value twice — once in the hook that normalizes and once in the hook that validates — would have let a mask that shortens a forged oversized value hide the length error it should have raised. Found while wiring the second hook; the two hooks now share one pipeline outcome.

The WCCS-022 proof first asserted the Suite's fields were on the checkout by reading the WC_Checkout singleton, which had already memoised its field array before the harness stored the document, so the assertion failed for the wrong reason. Fixed by building a fresh checkout instance per section, which also makes the harness exercise the real woocommerce_checkout_fields filter instead of a memo from before the schema existed.

json_encode(0.0) produces 0, so a zero of type float was stored as an integer and read back as one. Found by the WCCS-023 proof failing identically on both order backends with 'expected double(0) got integer(0)'. It is exactly the loss the acceptance names — a zero preserved in value but not in type — and it is invisible to assertEquals, because 0 == 0.0. Fixed by encoding with JSON_PRESERVE_ZERO_FRACTION, asserted on both backends and explained where the flag lives so a rewrite of that line knows why it is there.

An F00 exploratory payload shape for _wccs_fields ({field: {value, type, preset, schema_version}}) had been left in the record as if it were the design. It was a round-trip probe, not a format; the designed shape is {format, values} and the per-field snapshot belongs to WCCS-024. Recorded rather than silently replaced, because two shapes in the record for one meta key is how a format drifts.

Three WCCS-023 assertions were the harness being wrong rather than the code: two counted every meta row on the order when WooCommerce writes its own, and one expected the order's native billing field to be populated although the harness fires only the creation action, not WC_Checkout::create_order(). All three were rewritten to assert the intended claim — the plugin's own meta key, and that setting the native field the way WooCommerce does survives the Suite's write.

The value-to-label map of a field's options was constructed inside ClassicAdapter, interpreted independently by ChoiceFieldType::allowed_keys and needed a third time by the snapshot: three readers of one setting, and therefore three chances to disagree. Extracted as FieldDefinition::options(); the WCCS-021 proof, which compares the real field array WooCommerce builds, stayed green through the swap.

The WCCS-023 assertion that pinned the stored payload format at 1 had to be updated to 2, the same way the WCCS-022 hook-set assertion had to be updated in WCCS-023. Recorded because it is the recurring cost of an assertion that pins an exact value: it must be updated when the value changes deliberately, and that is what makes the pinning useful.

The WCCS-025 proof asserted that the bundle was hooked on wp_enqueue_scripts and failed with the hook present: the helper looked only for an instance-method callable, while a static method is registered as a class name. A verifier that knows half the callable shapes reports a hook as missing when it is there. Fixed to accept both, with the reason in the comment.

Two WCCS-021 assertions pinned a custom field's custom_attributes to exactly array( 'maxlength' => 14 ); the WCCS-025 marker joined them and both failed, correctly. Rewritten to assert by key, with a named assertion for the marker so it is a claim rather than a side effect of another one. Third consecutive task in which an assertion pinning an exact value caught a deliberate change.

F05.title: Presets Brasil, IMask e validação remota
F05.gate: Documento inválido não finaliza; CNPJ alfanumérico válido não é truncado nem convertido em número.
F05.why_gate_is_open: Only the first of the gate's two clauses can be proven yet, and only half of it. The second clause — an alphanumeric CNPJ is not truncated nor turned into a number — is met and asserted: the normalizer removes only recognised punctuation, keeps the letters, uppercases them and returns a string, and the fixture set contains the four documents that a `preg_replace( '/\D/' )` normalizer would silently corrupt. The first clause — an invalid document does not finish the checkout — needs validation that does not exist: check digits are WCCS-028's contract, and no preset names a validator, so a wrong CPF is normalized correctly and accepted. The phase gate closes with WCCS-028, which is also where ADR-0003's open question about alphanumeric check digits is to be settled against the official sources.
F05.way_forward: WCCS-027 applies the registered masks in the browser through the lifecycle WCCS-025 delivered; WCCS-028 implements the validators and settles ADR-0003's open question; WCCS-029 and WCCS-030 add the remote endpoint and the error interface. Nothing in the phase is blocked by CLASSIC-TEST-SURFACE for its implementation, but the gate's first clause is about a checkout refusing to finish, and observing that needs a rendered checkout — so the same decision that blocks F04 blocks the observation here too.
F05.detail: WCCS-026 delivered the Brazilian presets with contracts of their own. Each one now declares what the field is: the type it is built on, the mask it is typed with, the normalizer that turns what the customer typed into what the store keeps, and the settings the two need. The normalizer is the heart of it, and it is written against the line anybody would write — preg_replace( '/\D/', '', $value ) — which ADR-0003 forbids on this path and which passes the first case of every document while corrupting the rest: it turns an alphanumeric CNPJ into a different number, turns a CPF typed with a letter into a valid CPF nobody typed, and destroys the leading zeros of a postcode. The delivered normalizer removes only the punctuation these formats are written with, as a declared list rather than a character class, and leaves every other character intact for the validator to refuse. The fixtures exist to fail if that line is ever rewritten, and the shared file is read by both suites so the two sides cannot diverge. Three things are deliberately absent and each is asserted: no preset names a validator, because a key that is not registered would make every field built from the preset unsaveable and a key that exists but does nothing is a promise the code does not keep; RG declares no mask, because its format depends on the issuing state and inventing a national one was rejected; and no document preset uses a numeric type. Two defects were found. The mask guard rejected parentheses as code-shaped, which made the Brazilian telephone mask — written (00) 00000-0000 — impossible to register: parentheses are literal characters of a written format, and a mask definition is data consumed by the library and never evaluated, so the four genuinely code-shaped probes still fail while the telephone masks register. And the preset contract was being discarded before it reached the field: the picker passed defaults through, the type declared them and the catalogue published them, but buildField never read them and hardcoded a null normalizer, so the whole deliverable would have been inert and a merchant choosing CPF would have received a plain text field. Fixed with an allow-list, because a preset arrives from the server where any plugin can register one through a public hook: it may seed a mask and a normalizer and may not choose the field's identity, section, storage or visibility, which a test asserts by passing all of them and checking that none is obeyed. Two assertions belonging to earlier phases stopped testing what they claimed: WCCS-009 and WCCS-017 used br.cnpj and br.cpf as examples of unregistered keys, which was true while the Brazilian layer was a promise and became the opposite of the truth when this task registered them. Rewritten against a key that is absent by construction — the fourth task running in which an assertion pinning an exact value caught a deliberate change, and the first where what changed was a negative example. WCCS-027 applied the masks in the browser. IMask is a local dependency pinned to an exact version and bundled into the checkout bundle — sixty kilobytes, and the manifest WordPress receives still lists only jQuery and wp-i18n, so section 9's local-dependency rule is asserted rather than assumed. The task's real finding was measured rather than assumed: a mask created over an element that already holds a value formats it, and a mask created over an empty element does not reformat a value assigned afterwards. That makes the order the two components are registered in load-bearing — the value keeper restores first and the mask is built over the restored value — and with the order reversed a field replaced by a refresh comes back unformatted inside a masked input, which is precisely the failure the acceptance names. A test asserts the broken behaviour of the reversed order so that whoever reorders them finds out why. Paste, delete, autocomplete, cursor and refresh are covered in jsdom against a real DOM: a pasted value is formatted and one pasted too long is cut to the document's length, deleting the last digit reformats the rest, a value reported as input is formatted while one that arrives without an input event is left unformatted and not lost, and an element that survived the refresh keeps both its value and its cursor because nothing remasks a live input. The mobile half of the acceptance was thin until the keyboard was derived from the pattern itself: a digits-only mask asks for inputmode=numeric and the alphanumeric CNPJ mask deliberately does not, because a numeric keypad makes that document impossible to type — which is how a phone would break the value. One limitation is recorded rather than hidden: IMask's wildcard token matches any character, not an alphanumeric one, so the CNPJ mask is permissive in its data positions; tightening it would move a rule about what a document may contain into the browser, and the layer that owns that rule is the validator, which WCCS-028 delivers. Two of my own proof assertions were wrong and are recorded: the inline-script list carries an empty entry contributed by wp_set_script_translations, so indexing element zero read the wrong string, and do_item() prints the tag and returns a boolean, so assigning its return read one byte instead of the page.

defects_found_and_fixed: Mask::is_declarative() rejected parentheses as code-shaped, which made the Brazilian telephone masks — written (00) 00000-0000 and (00) 0000-0000 — impossible to register. Parentheses are literal characters of a written format, and a mask definition is data consumed by the mask library and never evaluated. Removed from the forbidden set with a regression asserting both telephone masks are declarative; the two genuinely code-shaped probes still fail.

The preset contract never reached the field it was meant to configure: FieldPicker passed `defaults` through, PickerChoice declared them, CatalogController published them, and buildField never read them — it hardcoded `normalizer: null` and took the mask only from the choice. Every Brazilian preset would have created a plain text field with a placeholder, and nothing in the preset's own unit tests could see it, because the defect was in the seam between what the server publishes and what the client applies. Fixed with an allow-list of the two keys a preset may seed.

Two assertions in earlier phases stopped testing what they claimed: WCCS-009 and WCCS-017 used br.cnpj and br.cpf as examples of unregistered keys, which was true while the Brazilian document layer was a promise and became the opposite of the truth once this task registered them. Rewritten against a key that is absent by construction, with the reason in the code.

The order the two checkout components are registered in decides whether a refresh keeps a field formatted: IMask formats a value an element already holds and does not reformat one assigned afterwards, so a mask built before the value was restored left the field unformatted inside a masked input. Measured rather than assumed, fixed by registering the keeper first, and pinned by a test that asserts the broken behaviour of the reversed order.

The mobile half of the acceptance had no implementation: IMask sets no inputmode, so a phone showed a general keyboard for a digits-only document. The keyboard is now derived from the pattern — numeric for a digits-only mask, and deliberately none for the alphanumeric CNPJ, where a numeric keypad would make the document impossible to type.

Two proof assertions were wrong: the inline-script list carries a falsy entry contributed by wp_set_script_translations at index zero, so 'exactly one entry at index zero' failed with the payload present; and do_item() prints the tag and returns a boolean, so assigning its return value measured one byte instead of the page. Both rewritten, and the printed tag is now captured with output buffering and asserted to be local.

gate_evidence.alphanumeric_cnpj_survives: WCCS-026: 12.ABC.345/01DE-35 becomes 12ABC34501DE35 — letters kept, uppercased, fourteen characters, a string, and not numeric

accept 8.2 as the effective floor and keep 8.3 only as a forward target

open_decisions.question: How will F04 be exercised when the site has no Classic Checkout page?
options: create an additional page with the [woocommerce_checkout] shortcode (change outside the plugin root)
open_decisions.recommendation: Request explicit authorization before creating or switching any checkout page.
open_decisions.observed: Recorded cost as of WCCS-022: two of the five F04 tasks are provable without it and are both met — WCCS-021 against the field array WooCommerce builds, WCCS-022 against its posted-data filter and its error collection, both reached through WooCommerce's own code. What it blocks is the part that needs a real request: the rendered form, the customer's POST through process_checkout(), and the order. WCCS-023 to WCCS-025 are expected to be provable without it too, because they concern what is written to the order rather than what is rendered. The gate itself cannot close without it.

open_decisions.question: Which runtime builds the frontend assets: the container or the host?
open_decisions.finding: Evidence from WCCS-006 makes the container option infeasible with the chosen toolchain: @wordpress/scripts 35.0.0 requires Node ^20.19.0 || >=22.13.0, and the php container runs Node 18.13.0.
open_decisions.provisional_choice: Build on the host (Node 22.21.1 / npm 10.9.4). WCCS-006 built successfully there.
open_decisions.to_close: Either accept host-only builds and pin the runtime in the repository, or upgrade the container Node version (a change outside the plugin root that needs authorization).
open_decisions.recommendation: Pin the runtime in the repository so local and CI builds agree, and record the container as unable to build until its Node is upgraded.

open_decisions.question: Can the two check digits of an alphanumeric CNPJ also be alphanumeric, or must they be digits?

open_decisions.recommendation: Resolve in WCCS-028 against the official sources (S9, S11), as ADR-0003 directs, and record the answer here. Until then no implementation may assert which is correct and no fixture may be treated as definitive.

closed_decisions.question: Where does the plugin source live under version control, given that the Devilbox repository ignores /data/www/* ?
closed_decisions.resolved_by: explicit instruction from the product owner
closed_decisions.decision: The plugin is its own Git repository at the plugin root, branch main. Nested inside an ignored path of the Devilbox checkout, which is harmless: that repository sees nothing under /data/www/*.
closed_decisions.correction: The belief that a roadmap entry had to be removed from .gitignore was wrong: no such rule existed anywhere. What made both the plugin and roadmap invisible was the Devilbox rule /data/www/*. The .gitignore now carries a note explaining why the planning is deliberately versioned, so the exclusion is not reintroduced by mistake.
closed_decisions.known_limitation: The repository is local and has no remote. Publishing requires a destination that has not been provided; CI is therefore versioned but still has not run.
closed_decisions.clean_checkout_needs_a_build: /build/ is not versioned, so a fresh clone needs npm install && npm run build before the admin screen works. That is the direct cost of not versioning generated output.
